name: Platform Work Directive
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: Commission forecasts plus model-based evidence from a similar Spanish law; transposition due December 2026
summary: The Commission expected 1.7-4.1 million people working through apps to be reclassified as employees and to earn up to EUR 484 million a year more. The final law left the test for employment status to national rules and applies only from late 2026, so nothing has been measured; a study of a similar Spanish law suggests more riders got contracts but overall rider work and pay fell.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement contains no indicators section; the memorandum refers to core indicators listed in the impact assessment and a review 5 years after entry into force

indicators.indicator: 1.7-4.1 million people reclassified as workers (of about 5.5 million at risk of misclassification among 28 million platform workers)
indicators.evidence: Not measured; transposition deadline 2 December 2026. The adopted text dropped the proposal's list of criteria for the presumption, leaving them to Member States, so the forecast may not hold. Model-based evidence from Spain's 2021 Riders' Law suggests reclassification raised the employee share but reduced riders' total work and wages.

indicators.indicator: Platform workers' earnings up to EUR 484m a year; up to EUR 4bn a year more tax and social contributions; platform costs EUR 1.9-4.5bn a year
Improved working conditions for 28 million people through transparency, human oversight and redress rights

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on improving working conditions in platform work (executive summary SWD(2021) 397), SWD(2021) 396
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on improving working conditions in platform work (executive summary SWD(2021) 397)
literature.outcomes: employment status; earnings; platform costs; public revenue
literature.headline: 1.7-4.1 million people reclassified as workers; earnings up to +EUR 484m a year; platform costs EUR 1.9-4.5bn a year, partly passed on; up to EUR 4bn a year extra public revenue
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected 1.7-4.1 million people working through apps to be reclassified as employees, gaining up to EUR 484 million a year, at a cost to platforms of EUR 1.9-4.5 billion a year.
literature.quality: forecast; based on the proposal's criteria, later dropped

literature.citation: Dolado, Jáñez & Wellschmied (2025), Riders on the Storm, IZA Discussion Paper 17740 (also CEPR DP19974)
literature.title: Riders on the Storm
literature.method: structural search-and-matching model calibrated to Spain's 2021 Riders' Law (presumption of employment)
literature.outcomes: employment; wages; welfare of delivery riders
literature.headline: Spain's presumption of employment for riders raised the share of employees but did not absorb the large outflow from self-employment and lowered riders' wages, causing welfare losses; adding a payroll tax cut for platforms hiring employees would preserve employment and raise welfare
literature.summary_plain: Spain's 2021 law presuming delivery riders are employees - a model for the EU Directive - increased the share of riders on employment contracts but, according to this model, cut overall rider jobs and wages.
literature.quality: model-based, not quasi-experimental; analogous national law
